## 2

I don’t doubt that you mean it, but the evidence points to a roughly spherical Earth—and you don’t have to trust space photos to check that.

For example, people in different parts of the world see different stars. As you travel south, Polaris gets lower in the northern sky until it disappears below the horizon, while southern constellations come into view. That’s what you’d expect when moving around a curved surface.

You can also compare the Sun’s angle at the same time in distant locations, an approach used to estimate Earth’s circumference more than 2,000 years ago.

What’s the strongest piece of evidence that convinced you the Earth is flat? We could look at what each model predicts and see which matches the observations.

## 3

Sunlight looks white, but it’s actually a mixture of colours. When it enters Earth’s atmosphere, it meets tiny molecules of nitrogen and oxygen. Those molecules scatter some of the light, sending it off in different directions.

Here’s the important part: they scatter short-wavelength light, like blue, much more strongly than long-wavelength light, like red. So when you look at the sky away from the Sun, lots of that scattered blue light reaches your eyes.

You might wonder: **why not violet, which has an even shorter wavelength?** Sunlight contains less violet than blue, and our eyes are less sensitive to violet. The combination looks blue to us.

At sunset, sunlight takes a much longer route through the atmosphere. Much of the blue gets scattered out of the direct beam before it reaches you, leaving the reds and oranges that make sunsets glow.

雨从入夜时落下，先是零星几滴，后来便密密地织满了街巷。路灯映着积水，像一封被揉皱的金色信笺。末班公交驶过，车轮推开薄薄的水浪，站牌下的人把伞又压低了一些。楼上的窗还亮着，厨房里传来碗筷轻碰的声音。我靠在窗边，看雨珠沿玻璃缓缓滑落。远处一扇门开了，又关上，只留下门前一小块温暖的光。夜色很深，杯里的茶却还热着。
